root.note: Latin cervēsia / cerevisia was itself a Celtic word; Wiktionary links it with Proto-Celtic *kurmi ‘beer’.

history: Romans drank wine and looked down on beer as a drink of the northern peoples. So when they needed a word for it, they took one from the Celts, whose word Latin wrote as cervēsia. In the west of the Empire the Latin word stayed: Portuguese cerveja, Spanish cerveza, Galician cervexa. France and Italy later took a Germanic word instead, bière and birra, like English beer. In Portugal ordering a draught beer has its own vocabulary, and it depends on the city. In Lisbon you ask for uma imperial, in Porto um fino, while uma caneca is a larger glass. Cerveja is the word for the drink itself.
historyEinfach: Cerveja means ‘beer’. The word is very old. The Romans took it from the Celts. Spanish cerveza comes from the same word. English beer comes from another word. In Lisbon a small glass of beer is uma imperial; in Porto it is um fino.

elsewhere.text: Spanish kept the same Celtic-Latin word.
Same drink, Germanic word. French bière and Italian birra took this one.
